She loves Tomas and has chosen him and the tenants over escape, carrying her mother’s lavender cloak, a knife, bread, a spare cloak, and copied evidence; she is cold, frightened, determined, and newly committed to open defiance.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Near the outer villages, Tomas has turned back from his attempted escape with Elianor to protect frightened tenants caught in an attack on a military convoy. He has been freed from Ashcombe’s cellar, still has his servant’s coat, stable tools, resistance knowledge, and scar near his jaw, and has arranged through Mara for messengers to guide eastern tenants to the quarry road. He loves Elianor, fears her association with him will destroy her, and is separated from her while trying to prevent soldiers and villagers from killing one another.

set.name: Lord Veyne
set.description: At Ashcombe manor, Lord Veyne remains nominal lord while Carrow’s garrison controls practical force. He has ordered Tomas imprisoned and authorized his execution after Elianor’s marriage, but does not yet know Tomas has escaped. He possesses the Veyne seal, estate ledgers, and authority over the stores; he knows of Elianor’s ledger alterations and is exhausted, fearful, defensive, and likely to seek reprisals when he learns of the convoy attack.

set.name: Lord Carrow
set.description: At Ashcombe manor with his military escort, Lord Carrow controls the garrison, roads, levy, and practical authority. He expects Tomas to be executed after Elianor’s marriage and remains unaware or not yet confirmed that Tomas has escaped. He possesses military power, wealth, political leverage, and command of the soldiers; he is cold, controlling, watchful, and increasingly threatened by resistance and the failed convoy operation.

set.name: Mara
set.description: At or near Ashcombe after helping Elianor free Tomas, Mara remains a longtime servant who knows the manor’s routines. She carried Tomas’s warning to Iven at the mill so resistance messengers could guide the eastern tenants to safety. She risks execution for aiding the lovers and the tenants, and remains loyal, practical, and afraid.
With help from the sympathetic maid Mara, Elianor freed Tomas from Ashcombe’s cellar prison and escaped the manor with him before dawn.
Before fleeing, Tomas sent a warning through Mara so resistance messengers could guide the eastern tenants toward the quarry road and away from the garrison.

A frightened tenant attack on a military convoy near the outer villages interrupted Elianor and Tomas’s flight; Tomas turned back to protect the villagers, and Elianor rode back toward Ashcombe to prevent reprisals.
Elianor must reach Ashcombe and use the Veyne seal or her evidence to oppose Lord Veyne’s reprisals against the tenant villages after the failed convoy attack.
Tomas and Elianor’s escape must fail at the outer villages, leaving Tomas separated from Elianor while he protects frightened tenants from soldiers and rebels.

chapters.name: The Manor Burns
chapters.content:
By the time Elianor saw Ashcombe’s towers, dawn had thinned the storm to a gray, needling rain. Her horse stumbled beneath her. Mud darkened the hem of her mother’s lavender cloak, and cold had stiffened the bread in her pocket. Still she urged the mare on.

Smoke lay over the lower fields.

At first she thought it was mist rising from the river. Then the wind shifted, and she saw the orange pulse beyond the alder trees. One cottage burned, then another. A third roof caught with a rush of sparks climbing into the low clouds.

“No,” she whispered.

The stable yard was crowded with soldiers. Their horses stamped and blew white clouds. Men carried torches despite the rain, while tenants stood at the far wall watching their homes burn. A woman held a child against her breast. Beside her, an old man had both hands raised, as though he could plead with the flames.

Elianor dismounted. “Where is my father?”

“On the steps,” answered a voice.

Lord Veyne stood beneath the portico in a wool coat thrown over his nightclothes. His face seemed to have collapsed inward since she had last seen him. Behind him, two officers watched with hands on their sword hilts.

“You ordered the villages burned,” Elianor said.

“I ordered a warning.”

“You ordered homes burned.”

“The convoy was attacked. Men are dead.”

“By frightened tenants who believed soldiers had come to seize their children for levy service.”

Her father’s anger covered his flinch. “You return after abandoning this house with a criminal, and presume to lecture me about order?”

She turned toward the fields. “Put out those fires.”

No one moved.

“You have no command here,” Lord Veyne said.

Elianor drew the Veyne seal from beneath her cloak. Her fingers were so cold she nearly dropped it. The stag of Ashcombe, stamped in dark red wax on its leather cord, caught the weak morning light.

“By authority of House Veyne,” she said, and her voice carried across the yard, “I command every soldier on this estate to stand down. No tenant home is to be touched. No prisoner is to be taken without written warrant.”

The soldiers looked toward their officers. The officers looked toward Lord Veyne.

For one breath, the old shape of the world held.

Then her father said, “That seal is mine.”

“It is the seal of the house.”

“And you are no longer my daughter in any way that matters.”

The words fell into the rain. Somewhere behind the manor, timber cracked as a roof gave way.

Lord Veyne descended one step. “You are disinherited, Elianor Veyne. Your dowry, lands, and name are forfeit. Take her to the west room. Lock the door.”

The older officer hesitated. “My lord—”

“Do it.”

Two guards seized her arms. Elianor twisted, striking one across the mouth with the seal. He cursed and tightened his grip. In the hall she saw Mara, pale beneath her cap, one hand pressed to her apron. Their eyes met briefly. Mara lowered her gaze.

That was not surrender. Elianor knew the difference now.

They dragged her upstairs. A latch lifted somewhere. A bucket fell. From below came the deep crash of a table overturned.

The west room had been her mother’s sewing chamber. They pushed Elianor inside and locked the door. She tested the barred window, then sat on the floor and listened.

The manor changed around her.

Orders were shouted. Boots ran. In the kitchens, crockery shattered. Once, a soldier cried out, followed by the furious voice of a cook who had apparently struck him with a ladle. From the yard came a chant, quiet but steady.

“Open the stores! Open the stores!”

Her father believed fear made obedience. He had not understood that fear, carried far enough, became a thing people shared. Shared fear could become courage.

Near midday, horns sounded from the road. Carrow’s reinforcements had arrived.

A key turned in her door. A captain entered with two soldiers. “Lord Carrow requests your presence.”

“I refuse.”

“He does not request.”

Before he reached her, the window burst inward. A brick struck the wall beside his head. As the soldiers turned, Elianor seized the captain’s sword belt, drove her knee into his thigh, and ran into the corridor.

Mara waited at the stairhead.

“This way,” she breathed.

“How?”

“Servants have many doors. Lords notice only the grand ones.”

They plunged through the laundry passage. A groom had left a back door unbarred; two kitchen maids held it against a soldier while the old gardener dragged a cart across the threshold. Mara shoved Elianor through, then dropped the bar.

The village square roared with voices.

Carrow’s soldiers had formed a line between the manor and the tenants. Families crowded around carts, children hidden beneath blankets. On the northern road, figures appeared through the rain—rebels carrying mismatched weapons, coming fast.

A soldier raised his crossbow.

“Lower it!” Elianor shouted, stepping into the open. “They are tenants, not an enemy army.”

Carrow turned in his saddle. His black cloak was dry beneath a waxed mantle, his expression untouched by the weather or the fires behind him.

“You have made a dramatic return,” he said. “The betrothal agreement grants me authority over this estate.”

“It grants you nothing over unarmed families.”

“It grants me authority where your father has failed.”

The rebels entered the square. A young man at their front lifted a sword. Soldiers leveled pikes. Between them, a child began to sob.

Elianor climbed onto the fountain ledge. “Listen! Lower your weapons. Let the tenants leave by the south road. Carrow’s men may withdraw to the manor. The rebels may take the stores without bloodshed.”

For a moment, the impossible seemed to wait upon her words.

Then Tomas broke from the edge of the square.

His servant’s coat was torn, and blood ran from his brow. He had one arm around a tenant boy and was pushing two armed villagers apart with the other.

“Not here!” he shouted. “There are children!”

A rebel mistook the movement for an attack and lunged. Tomas caught the blade on a length of wood, but soldiers closed around him. He fought like a man who had forgotten he could be tired. One struck his wounded shoulder. Another twisted his arms behind him.

“Elianor!”

She leaped from the fountain. Carrow seized her wrist.

“Stay where you are,” he murmured. “You have already lost enough.”

Tomas looked at her across the widening space. His face held no fear for himself, only the fear that she would be destroyed beside him.

“Do not bargain for me,” he called.

The soldiers dragged him toward the manor as the rebels surged forward and the square dissolved into shouting. Elianor tore against Carrow’s grip, her mother’s cloak opening like a lavender wing in the rain.

Behind them, Ashcombe burned. Ahead, the rebellion came on. Tomas was carried between them, bound and bleeding, while Elianor understood that the fire had reached the last place in the kingdom where she had believed herself safe.

set.name: Elianor Veyne
set.description: At Ashcombe’s village square after escaping confinement with Mara, Elianor is held by Carrow while Tomas is dragged toward the manor in chains. She has publicly denounced her father’s reprisals, used the Veyne seal to command a stand-down, and been declared disinherited. She loves Tomas and remains committed to protecting tenants and civilians; she intends to resist Carrow, free or defend Tomas, and prevent a massacre. She possesses her mother’s lavender cloak, the Veyne seal, a knife, and copied evidence/altered-ledger knowledge. She is cold, frightened, furious, and resolute.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Captured and being taken toward Ashcombe manor after the village-square confrontation, Tomas is bound and bleeding from a head wound and a struck shoulder. He turned back from escape to protect frightened tenants and has now been seized while separating armed villagers and rebels from civilians. He loves Elianor, fears her destruction through association with him, and wants the tenants and children kept alive. He retains his servant’s coat, scar near his jaw, stable tools, and resistance knowledge, though his movement and freedom are restricted.

set.name: Lord Veyne
set.description: At Ashcombe manor, Lord Veyne remains nominal lord but has lost practical control to Carrow’s garrison and rising servant and tenant resistance. He ordered tenant homes burned as a warning, rejected Elianor’s seal-command, declared her disinherited, and confined her, unaware until the square crisis that Tomas had escaped and been recaptured. He possesses the estate ledgers, hidden grain authority, and formal Veyne power, while Carrow controls the soldiers. He is exhausted, defensive, angry, and increasingly desperate to preserve order and himself.

set.name: Lord Carrow
set.description: At Ashcombe’s village square with reinforcements and soldiers, Lord Carrow claims authority over the estate through the betrothal agreement. He controls the garrison, roads, levy, and immediate force, has Elianor in his grasp, and has Tomas captured and being returned to the manor. He intends to suppress the rebels, preserve his political claim, and compel obedience; he regards Elianor’s defiance as a threat. He is cold, controlled, militarily confident, and watchful.

set.name: Mara
set.description: At Ashcombe, Mara helped Elianor escape the west-room confinement through servant passages and remains aligned with Elianor and the resisting household. She knows the manor’s hidden routes and routines, previously aided Tomas’s escape, and risks execution if Carrow’s soldiers identify her role. She wants to protect Elianor, Tomas, and the tenants. She is frightened, practical, and actively defiant.
Elianor returned to Ashcombe during the storm and found Lord Veyne’s soldiers burning tenant homes as reprisals for the failed convoy attack.
Elianor publicly used the Veyne seal to order the soldiers to stand down, but Lord Veyne declared her disinherited and had her confined in the west room.
Ashcombe’s servants and tenants began openly resisting the household and garrison, including obstructing soldiers and demanding that the hidden stores be opened.
Lord Carrow arrived with reinforcements and claimed authority over Ashcombe through the betrothal agreement.
Elianor escaped confinement with Mara’s help and reached the village square, where Carrow’s soldiers faced tenants and the approaching rebel force.
Tomas was captured while trying to keep rebels and soldiers from attacking civilians in the village square.
Carrow must establish a military tribunal at Ashcombe and charge Tomas with treason and inciting rebellion using largely fabricated evidence.
Elianor must escape Carrow’s custody, demand a public hearing, and use the hidden ledgers and her testimony to expose Lord Veyne’s unlawful grain and reprisal orders.
The rebels’ pressure on Ashcombe must threaten a violent assault, forcing Elianor to negotiate a surrender to protect soldiers, tenants, and household workers.

chapters.name: A Traitor’s Trial
chapters.content:
The manor doors closed on the rain and the shouting.

Tomas was taken through the entrance hall with his wrists bound behind him. Blood had dried at his temple, black beneath the yellow light of the sconces. Elianor saw him only for a moment before Carrow’s men forced her into the old music room and posted a guard outside.

“Where are you taking him?” she demanded.

“To judgment,” Carrow said.

“You have no court here.”

“I have soldiers, a prisoner, and a rebellion at the gates. That is sufficient.”

He left her with the door locked.

For an hour she heard the manor being transformed. Tables scraped across the great hall floor. Men hammered boards over the windows facing the village. From beyond the walls came the dull, repeated sound of horns: the rebels calling to one another in the rain. Ashcombe was surrounded.

Mara reached Elianor through the servant’s hatch behind the music room’s tapestry. Her cap was gone, and a cut crossed her cheek.

“They are filling the hall,” she whispered. “Carrow calls it a military tribunal.”

“Who sits in judgment?”

“His captain. A lieutenant. Your father.”

“Three men who have already chosen the verdict.”

Mara swallowed. “They have Tomas tied to a chair. The captain has brought out irons.”

The room seemed to contract around Elianor. She touched the Veyne seal beneath her cloak. Its edge pressed into her palm.

“Then open the door.”

“Mara—”

“Servants have many doors,” Mara said, repeating herself from the escape, though her voice shook. “Lords notice only the grand ones.”

She returned with a ring of keys. The guard outside had been called to the hall. Elianor stepped into the corridor and ran.

The great hall smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and blood. Tomas sat beneath the carved Veyne stag, his hands lashed to the arms of a chair. Two soldiers stood behind him. His coat had been cut open at the shoulder, and the bruising there was already darkening.

At the high table, Carrow had placed a sheet of parchment before himself.

“Lady Elianor,” he said. “You interrupt a lawful proceeding.”

“Lawful?” She walked into the center of the hall. “Name the law that permits an invading lord to judge a man in the house of the man he means to seize.”

Carrow’s expression barely changed. “Tomas Ardan is charged with treason against the crown, murder of six soldiers at the eastern convoy, and inciting rebellion among Ashcombe’s tenants.”

A murmur passed through the servants gathered along the walls.

Elianor looked at the parchment. “The convoy soldiers were killed after they fired on villagers.”

“Your sympathy for criminals is well established.”

“Then hear the witnesses.”

Carrow gestured to the captain. “Remove her.”

Lord Veyne rose from his place. He seemed smaller than he had that morning, wrapped in a coat too large for him. “Elianor, do not make this worse.”

“You made it worse when you hid grain and called your tenants thieves for being hungry.”

His face blanched.

She drew the copied ledgers from inside her cloak. The pages were creased and damp, but the columns remained legible. She held them high.

“Here are Ashcombe’s true stores, marked in my father’s hand. Here are the false shortages sent to the capital. Here are the shipments sold to Carrow’s quartermaster while children starved in the lower village.”

The captain laughed. “Forged.”

“Ask the steward.”

The old steward stood near the hearth, trembling. Lord Veyne turned toward him.

“Say nothing,” he ordered.

The steward looked at the tenants packed beyond the doors. “The lady speaks true.”

The hall erupted. Soldiers raised pikes. A woman cried that her sons had died in the snow while the manor’s bins were full. Someone shouted for the doors to be opened.

Carrow struck the table with his fist. “Silence!”

No one obeyed.

Elianor faced the tribunal. “You want testimony? Hear mine. My father ordered the burning of tenant homes as punishment for the convoy attack. I saw the fires. I heard him call them a warning. He used soldiers to enforce unlawful levies and concealed food while claiming famine. If Tomas is guilty of resisting that cruelty, then his guilt is shared by every person who has refused to kneel.”

Tomas lifted his head. “Elianor.”

She did not look away from him. If she did, she feared she would lose the strength to continue.

Carrow’s captain approached with the irons. “The prisoner will confess before sunset.”

“No,” Elianor said.

The captain seized her arm. Tomas surged against the ropes, and one of the soldiers struck him across the mouth.

Something broke loose in her—not courage, exactly, but the last remnant of fear’s authority.

She tore the seal from her neck and held it toward the hall. “By the authority of House Veyne, I command that no torture be performed on this estate.”

The captain hesitated.

Carrow stood. “That authority was revoked.”

“Then why are you so eager to silence it?”

Outside, a horn sounded three times. A rebel voice called from beyond the walls: “Open Ashcombe, or we take it stone by stone!”

The soldiers glanced toward the shuttered windows. The tenants began pounding on the doors.

Lord Veyne pointed at his daughter. “Confine her. She is no longer my heir, no longer mistress here, and no longer fit to bear the Veyne name.”

Two guards moved toward her.

Elianor stepped back until she stood beside Tomas. The ropes between them were rough and stained, but she placed her hand over his bound fingers.

“I renounce it,” she said.

The words seemed to quiet even the storm.

“I renounce the title, the inheritance, and every privilege that required another person to bow. I will not stand before Tomas as a noblewoman pleading for a servant’s life. I stand beside him as his equal.”

Tomas’s fingers tightened against hers.

Carrow’s gaze sharpened. “You believe words can change what you are?”

“No,” Elianor answered. “I believe what I do can.”

The guards seized her. Mara shouted from the crowd, and the kitchen servants surged forward with knives, ladles, and broken chair legs. The soldiers leveled their weapons, but several lowered them rather than fire.

Lord Veyne stared at the disorder as if it were a judgment more terrible than any court. “You have destroyed this family.”

Elianor was dragged toward the side passage. “No, Father. I only stopped pretending it was innocent.”

They locked her in the chapel vestibule, where her mother’s grave lay beyond an iron screen. Through the stone she heard Carrow ordering the gates barred, heard Tomas being taken below, and heard the rebels answer with the first heavy blows against Ashcombe’s outer doors.

The tribunal had ended without a verdict. The siege had begun in earnest.

In the dimness, Elianor pressed her forehead to the cold iron and prayed for one thing only: that the people inside and outside the walls would live long enough to see morning.

set.name: Elianor Veyne
set.description: In Ashcombe’s chapel vestibule under guard, beside her dead mother’s chapel, Elianor has publicly exposed the hidden grain records and her father’s unlawful reprisal orders, saved Tomas from immediate torture, and renounced her title and inheritance. She stands openly as Tomas’s equal and seeks to prevent the rebels’ assault from becoming a massacre of civilians, servants, or soldiers. She knows the tribunal is fabricated, Tomas is being held below, and Carrow controls the garrison while the rebels surround the manor. She possesses her mother’s lavender cloak, the Veyne seal, knife, copied ledgers, and altered-ledger knowledge. She is exhausted, frightened, grieving, defiant, and confined but morally resolute.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Held prisoner below Ashcombe manor after the failed tribunal, Tomas remains bound and injured, with a head wound, bruised shoulder, and split mouth. He has been charged falsely with treason, murder, and inciting rebellion; Elianor’s testimony prevented immediate torture, and he heard her renounce her title to stand beside him as an equal. He wants Elianor and the civilians protected and still seeks a way to stop the siege from becoming slaughter. He retains his servant’s coat and scar near his jaw, while his stable tools and resistance knowledge are inaccessible or restricted. He is frightened for Elianor, in pain, and determined.

set.name: Lord Veyne
set.description: Inside Ashcombe manor, Lord Veyne has lost his remaining political standing after the steward confirmed his concealed grain and falsified shortages. He remains nominal lord but is subordinated to Carrow’s military authority; he ordered Elianor confined again after she exposed him and renounced the Veyne name. He wants to preserve order, himself, and what remains of his family legacy, though he now sees Elianor as the destroyer of the family. He knows the manor is surrounded, servants are resisting, and Tomas remains imprisoned. He possesses formal estate records and residual Veyne authority but is exhausted, horrified, defensive, and powerless.

set.name: Lady Veyne
set.description: Dead and buried in the Veyne family chapel; her lavender-scented cloak remains Elianor’s possession and comfort. Elianor is now confined in the chapel vestibule beside her grave while Ashcombe is besieged.

set.name: Lord Carrow
set.description: Inside Ashcombe manor directing the garrison and controlling the military tribunal, Carrow has charged Tomas with fabricated crimes, ordered the gates barred, and resisted Elianor’s public evidence and seal-command. He still claims authority through the betrothal agreement and intends to suppress the rebels, retain control of the estate, and prevent Elianor’s defiance from weakening him. He knows the rebels are battering the outer doors and that soldiers and servants are wavering. He possesses military command, tribunal authority, and the betrothal claim. He is controlled, angry, watchful, and increasingly threatened.

set.name: Mara
set.description: Inside Ashcombe with the resisting household, Mara helped Elianor escape into the tribunal and stood with the servants when soldiers tried to seize her. She knows the manor’s hidden routes and routines, aided Tomas before, and remains committed to protecting Elianor, Tomas, and civilians. She has no weapon specified beyond access to servant passages and the household’s improvised weapons. She is frightened, wounded by a cut across her cheek, and actively defiant as the siege begins.
Carrow convened a military tribunal in Ashcombe’s great hall and charged Tomas Ardan with treason, murder of six soldiers, and inciting rebellion, while preparing torture to force a confession.
Ashcombe’s steward corroborated Elianor’s copied ledgers, confirming Lord Veyne concealed grain and falsified shortages for the capital and Carrow’s quartermaster.
Elianor publicly renounced the Veyne title and inheritance, declaring that she would stand beside Tomas as his equal rather than plead for a servant’s life.
The tribunal collapsed without a verdict as servants resisted inside Ashcombe and rebels began battering the estate’s outer doors.

chapters.name: The Last Mercy
chapters.content:
By morning, the chapel windows were white with frost. Elianor woke with her cheek against the iron screen and the taste of blood where she had bitten it in sleep.

The blows against Ashcombe’s outer doors had continued through the night. Each one traveled through the stone beneath her. Between them came shouts, the scrape of furniture dragged into barricades, and once the crack of a musket. Then silence. Then another horn from the rebels.

Mara opened the chapel door after dawn. Her cheek was bound with linen. In one hand she carried bread; in the other, a ring of keys.

“Eat,” she said.

“Where is Tomas?”

“Below. I heard the gaoler say Carrow means to move him.”

“Move him where?”

“He did not say.”

Elianor took the bread. She could not swallow. “Then we must make them speak.”

They found the great hall crowded with men who had not slept. Carrow stood before the windows, studying the rebel banners beyond the frozen moat. His soldiers held the doors, though several watched the servants with the unease of men who understood that a house could turn against them from within.

Lord Veyne sat beneath the carved stag. He had aged ten years since the tribunal, his hands trembling on the arms of his chair.

Elianor lifted the Veyne seal. “You have lost the walls, the stores, and the loyalty of this household. You have one thing left to bargain with: the lives inside them.”

Carrow turned. “You renounced the authority that seal represents.”

“I renounced its privileges. I did not renounce its debts.” She faced the nearest captain. “Open the gates. Let the household workers leave unharmed. Let soldiers who lay down their arms pass out without pursuit. Let the tenants take what grain they can carry.”

A young soldier glanced at Carrow. “My lord, the men have had no relief since yesterday.”

Carrow’s mouth hardened. “The rebels will butcher them.”

“They may,” Elianor said. “Or they may spare them if you stop giving them reasons to believe everyone here is your accomplice.”

A kitchen woman stepped forward. “My sons are in the lower village. I will not die for a lord who hid flour from us.”

The steward joined her. “There are forty-seven servants and nineteen soldiers who have not drawn blood.”

Elianor crossed to the writing table. With a shaking hand, she wrote the terms on the back of a tax inventory: household workers, unarmed soldiers, and noncombatants would leave by the south gate; the estate stores would be opened; no surrendered man would be hanged or pressed into service. She signed, then sealed it.

The captain read the page. “And Lord Carrow?”

“He remains to answer for the tribunal and unlawful executions.”

Carrow laughed softly. “You negotiate as though you possess a future.”

“No,” she replied. “I negotiate because they do.”

Perhaps it was hunger in the room, or the sight of soldiers lowering their eyes. Carrow snatched the paper from the captain and signed.

The south gate opened near noon. Servants went first, carrying only blankets and the clothes they wore. Soldiers followed with their weapons stacked on the flagstones. Rebel archers watched from the ridge, bows lowered but ready. No one was stopped. No one was struck.

Then Mara pulled Elianor from the gate. “He is not among them.”

Elianor found Tomas in the old stable loft. Carrow had moved him through a servant passage during the surrender. His wrists were bound before him, his face a map of bruises. A rope lay coiled beside a soldier.

For a moment Elianor could not breathe.

“Tomas.”

His split mouth tried to smile. “You always did find the difficult door.”

The soldier stepped between them. “You have five minutes.”

“Leave us,” Elianor said.

“He ordered—”

She held up the signed surrender. “Are you surrendered?”

The soldier looked toward the stair, then out at the rebels below. At last he set down his spear and walked away.

Elianor knelt. Tomas smelled of cold, blood, and hay.

“Carrow means to hang you before the gates fall.”

“I know.”

“I can offer myself.”

“No.”

“As hostage. As prisoner. As his wife, if that is what he thinks will save him.”

Tomas shook his head. “There is no bargain with a man who has decided our lives are coins.”

She clasped his hands. “We could have had time.”

His eyes closed. “A little house. Two rooms, perhaps three if we were foolish. A roof that did not leak.”

“And a garden.”

“You hate gardening.”

“I hate being told what to plant.”

“Then nothing in rows. Apples wherever they pleased. Beans along the fence. You could ride the roads and come home when you wanted.”

“To you.”

“To us.”

A bell began ringing in the courtyard.

“I would have learned every road,” she whispered.

“And I would have chosen my work. Not stable work because a lord required it. Not fighting because a king named my father a rebel. Something with wood, perhaps. Or horses, if they improved their manners.”

The loft door opened. Carrow stood there with two soldiers.

“Take me instead,” Elianor said.

“I have taken enough from you already,” Carrow answered. “Your father’s name, your estate, your protection. Tomas is the only thing left that might frighten the rebels.”

“He is a man, not a message.”

“Today he is both.”

They dragged Tomas down. Elianor followed, threatening him with the seal and every witness to the surrender. In the courtyard, a gallows had been made from a cart axle and a beam torn from the granary.

The rebels saw him. A roar rose beyond the walls.

Elianor threw herself before Carrow. “If you hang him, they will take this manor stone by stone.”

“They will take it whether he lives or dies.”

“Then let me stand there.”

Carrow nodded. Soldiers seized her arms.

Tomas climbed the steps without help. At the top he turned toward her. Snow began whitening his dark hair.

“I am here,” she said.

“I know.”

The hood covered his face. Elianor screamed his name. The trap gave way.

For one heartbeat the courtyard held still.

Then the outer doors exploded inward.

Rebels poured through smoke and splintered wood. Soldiers broke formation; some fled through the open gate, others threw down their weapons. Carrow drew his sword and fought toward the manor steps, shouting for men who no longer answered. A spear caught him beneath the ribs. He fell against the frozen stones as the rebels surged past.

Elianor tore free and ran to Tomas. Mara was already cutting the rope. Elianor caught him as he dropped, lowering him into the snow. His head settled beneath her chin. She pressed her fingers to his throat, though she knew.

Around them Ashcombe was being taken. The gates stood open. Grain carts rolled from the stores. Men shouted victory into the smoke.

Tomas did not hear it.

Elianor held him beneath the gallows, his bloodless face against her mother’s lavender cloak, and understood that victory was not the opposite of loss. It was only what the living called the world after the dead had been taken from it.

set.name: Elianor Veyne
set.description: At Ashcombe’s courtyard beneath the gallows after the rebel breach, Elianor is holding Tomas’s dead body. She has renounced her title and inheritance but still possesses the Veyne seal, her mother’s lavender cloak, knife, and copied ledgers. She secured a limited surrender that let many servants, noncombatants, and unarmed soldiers leave unharmed, and she now knows Carrow secretly ordered Tomas’s execution and was killed by a rebel spear. Elianor’s love for Tomas remains absolute; she is devastated, exhausted, and unable to find consolation in the rebel victory, but must survive and honor his request to use the remaining Veyne wealth and stores for the villages.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Dead in Ashcombe’s courtyard beneath the gallows. Carrow had him secretly executed after refusing Elianor’s offer to exchange herself for his life. He died still committed to protecting Elianor and civilians, and had urged her to survive, use the family wealth to help the villages, and choose a life beyond inherited duty. His body is in Elianor’s arms; his servant’s coat, scars, and injuries remain visible.

set.name: Lord Veyne
set.description: Inside Ashcombe or removed under the surrender as the manor falls; Lord Veyne’s exact fate is unresolved. His political standing and estate authority are destroyed, his concealed grain and unlawful orders have been exposed, and Elianor has renounced him and the Veyne inheritance. He is exhausted, horrified, defensive, and powerless while the rebels take control.

set.name: Lady Veyne
set.description: Dead and buried in the Veyne family chapel. Her lavender-scented cloak was Elianor’s comfort during the siege and now covers Tomas’s body in the courtyard. Her memory remains emotionally central to Elianor.

set.name: Lord Carrow
set.description: Dead in Ashcombe’s courtyard after fighting the rebels during the breach. He refused to release Tomas, secretly ordered his hanging before the rebels could seize the manor, and tried to use Tomas’s death to frighten the rebel force. His military command and betrothal claim are ended.

set.name: Mara
set.description: At Ashcombe after the rebel breach, having helped Elianor reach Tomas and cut him down from the gallows. She remains loyal to Elianor and committed to protecting civilians and the household, though she is frightened, wounded across the cheek, and now amid the confused aftermath of the manor’s fall.

Elianor secured Carrow’s signed surrender terms, opening Ashcombe’s south gate so unarmed soldiers, household workers, and other noncombatants could leave unharmed while the estate stores were opened.
Carrow secretly hanged Tomas in Ashcombe’s courtyard, and rebel forces breached the manor immediately afterward; Carrow was killed in the fighting while Elianor held Tomas’s body beneath the gallows.

After Ashcombe falls, Elianor must place the surviving Veyne inheritance, grain reserves, and estate lands under communal control while working to feed and protect the liberated villages despite distrust of her family name.

chapters.name: What the Living Owe
chapters.content:
## What the Living Owe

By the third morning after Ashcombe fell, snowmelt ran black through the courtyard gutters, carrying ash and straw into the ditches. The gallows stood empty beneath a torn canvas sheet, but its shape remained a wound in the middle of the estate.

Elianor had not slept. She had washed Tomas’s blood from her hands, though it seemed to have entered the lines of her palms. Mara found her in the great hall with her mother’s lavender cloak folded across her knees.

“You must eat,” Mara said.

“I know.”

“You have said that for two days.”

Beyond the windows, men and women carried sacks from the opened stores. A council of tenants, rebels, and two deserters now controlled the estate. For the first time in years, no one waited for Lord Veyne’s permission to open a door.

That freedom frightened Elianor almost as much as obedience had.

Before noon, a rider came from the eastern road. Lord Veyne had been found beside his wife’s tomb and had surrendered without resistance. Some demanded a trial for the burned cottages and hidden grain; others wanted him exchanged for prisoners. No one called him lord except as an accusation.

Elianor gave the messenger her father’s signet.

“Tell the council it is not mine to decide his sentence,” she said. “Let the villages name witnesses. Let the evidence be kept openly. Justice must not become another word for revenge.”

That afternoon, the council met in the steward’s room. The ledgers lay across the table, their pages swollen with damp. Elianor placed beside them the deeds to Ashcombe’s fields, the mill, the house, the winter stores, and the silver hidden in her father’s chest.

Hobb, the old tenant, stared at the papers. “You mean to give it all away?”

“No. I mean to stop one family from owning what hundreds have made and maintained.”

A young farmer with a bandaged ear laughed. “A fine distinction from a Veyne.”

The words hurt, but Elianor did not turn from him.

“You are right to distrust me,” she said. “I ate from stores while your children starved. I wore silk made by hands that could not afford bread. I believed kindness from inside the house could excuse the house itself.”

“The land will be held by village councils,” she continued. “The mill and stores will be managed in common. The house may become a hospital, school, or meeting place, as the people decide. My mother’s jewelry and the silver will buy seed, tools, and medicine. I will not govern this. I will work where I am told.”

“Why?” Hobb asked.

Because Tomas had told her to survive. Because love, ending only in mourning, was another kind of possession. Because what had been taken from the villages could not be made clean by one woman’s remorse.

“Because it is owed,” she said.

They did not trust her that day. They took the documents. That was enough.

Weeks passed. The roads opened in patches, bringing news from Valedain: garrisons abandoning towns, noble families locking their gates, councils forming wherever soldiers had been driven out. In some places, old banners returned by night. In others, hunger made a new tyrant of whoever controlled the granary. Liberation was not a door but a field full of traps.

Elianor hauled sacks until her shoulders bruised. She helped Mara inventory blankets and rode to villages that had once sent petitions to Ashcombe and now met her with axes. Sometimes they let her speak. Sometimes they did not. She kept going.

At the first thaw, they held a memorial in the village square. Names were read from rough boards: tenants burned in their homes, soldiers killed while obeying orders or refusing them, children lost to winter, and rebels fallen at Ashcombe’s gates. The list continued until the reader’s voice broke.

Tomas Ardan’s name was near the end.

Elianor stood before the crowd wearing no jewels or family colors, only a plain wool coat over her mother’s lavender cloak. Some had loved Tomas as a comrade. Some had known him as a stable servant. Others knew only that he had died beneath a nobleman’s gallows.

“I will not call Tomas a martyr belonging to one faction,” she said. “He belonged to no banner more than he belonged to the people he protected. He was my beloved, but also a son, a brother, a worker, and a man who understood that pity is not enough.”

The wind moved through the bare branches.

“He taught me that compassion without justice leaves the powerful untouched. He taught me that a gift becomes an insult when the giver keeps the right to take it back. He taught me to ask what the living owe the dead—not prayers alone, but a world less cruel than the one that killed them.”

Her grief did not lessen. It became a road beneath her feet.

At dawn the next day, Elianor saddled a gray mare from the communal stable. Mara watched from the yard, her cheek scar pale in the morning light.

“Where are you going?”

“The north villages. The seed carts are late.”

“You could rest.”

Elianor touched the worn reins. She saw Tomas beside a ruined road, smiling as though the horizon had promised him something. She could not follow him there. She could only carry what he had given her into days he would never see.

“I will rest when the work is done,” she said, though they both knew it would never be done.

She rode beyond the rebuilt houses as the sun rose over Valedain. Behind her, hammers rang, children called, and smoke lifted from cook fires. Ahead waited hunger, quarrels, failing stores, and men who would try to rebuild the old world under new names.

Elianor turned her horse toward them.

Tomas’s memory traveled with her—not as a chain or consolation, but as a question she would spend the rest of her life answering.

set.name: Elianor Veyne
set.description: At dawn after the first thaw, Elianor has renounced her title and refuses restoration of Veyne authority. She lives and works under the direction of the village councils, hauling grain, inventorying communal supplies, and riding between villages to address shortages. She possesses her mother’s lavender cloak, the Veyne seal surrendered to the council, copied ledgers, and plain clothing rather than jewels. She is permanently grieving Tomas but emotionally steadied by his teachings, distrustful of inherited power, committed to communal justice, and facing suspicion because of her family name. She is riding north from the rebuilt village to find delayed seed carts, determined to help remake Valedain rather than rule it.

set.name: Tomas
set.description: Dead in Ashcombe’s courtyard beneath the gallows. Tomas was secretly hanged by Carrow before the rebel breach and died committed to protecting Elianor and civilians. His memory is honored at the village memorial not as property of a faction but as that of a servant, son, beloved, and teacher whose insistence on justice shapes Elianor’s lifelong work. His body has been mourned and his coat, scars, and injuries remain part of Elianor’s memory.

set.name: Lord Veyne
set.description: Lord Veyne surrendered without resistance beside Lady Veyne’s tomb after Ashcombe fell. His authority, title in practice, wealth, and estate control are destroyed; village councils hold evidence of his concealed grain and unlawful orders and will determine his sentence through an open process. He is disgraced, powerless, and awaiting judgment.

set.name: Lady Veyne
set.description: Dead and buried in the Veyne family chapel. Her lavender cloak remains Elianor’s principal keepsake and was worn beneath a plain coat at Tomas’s memorial. Her memory continues to connect Elianor to tenderness, loss, and the moral inheritance she is trying to transform.

set.name: Lord Carrow
set.description: Dead in Ashcombe’s courtyard during the rebel breach after ordering Tomas’s execution and refusing Elianor’s exchange. His military command and betrothal claim are ended, and his forces have been defeated or withdrawn. He has no remaining influence over Elianor, Tomas, Ashcombe, or Valedain.

set.name: Mara
set.description: At the rebuilt village and communal Ashcombe settlement, Mara works beside Elianor to inventory blankets and supplies and protect civilians. Her cheek bears a pale scar from the fighting. She remains loyal but practical, urging Elianor to rest while supporting her work among people who distrust the Veyne name; she knows the rebuilding will be difficult and ongoing.
After Ashcombe fell, Lord Veyne surrendered at the Veyne family tomb and the villages began gathering evidence to determine his sentence openly.
Elianor transferred the Veyne deeds, fields, mill, house, silver, jewelry, and grain stores to village councils and communal management for food, seed, tools, medicine, and public use.
Elianor publicly acknowledged that Tomas taught her compassion without justice was insufficient, and memorialized him among civilians, soldiers, and rebels killed in the uprising.
Elianor began working as a communal laborer and traveling between villages to address shortages, carrying Tomas’s memory into the uncertain rebuilding of Valedain.

They rode beyond the southern fields, through snow that erased their tracks. The storm thinned as they crossed a ridge. Below lay a valley of blackened stones and collapsed chimneys, houses reduced to ash. A dead orchard stood among them, branches twisted like fingers.

Tomas dismounted. “This was Darrin’s Ford.”
errors.pair: He rubbed Bracken’s wet neck. “I grew up near the eastern border. A village called Darrin’s Ford.”
